slides.title: Files and Directories

blocks.text: Every operating system, such as Windows or Linux, comes with a file system for storing files.
The file system is organized as a tree of directories.
Every file is placed in a directory in the file system.
The root of the file system starts with a drive letter, such as c:\ on the Windows OS, or slash / on the Linux OS.
Directory names are separated by backslash \ on Windows, or slash / on the Linux OS.

slides.title: Absolute versus Relative File Names

blocks.text: An absolute file name contains the complete directory path
c:\Users\mudawar\Documents\JavaCode\src\Welcome.java
is an absolute file name on the Windows OS.
/home/mudawar/JavaCode/src/Welcome.java is an absolute
file name on the Linux OS.
A relative file name starts at the current working directory and does not include the complete directory path.
Welcome.java is a relative file name in the src directory.
src/Welcome.java is a relative name in the JavaCode directory.

slides.title: The File class

blocks.text: The File class provides an abstraction that deals with file and directory path names in a machine-independent fashion.
The File class contains the methods for obtaining the properties of a file or directory, and for renaming and deleting a file or directory.
However, the File class does not contain the methods for reading and writing file contents.
The file name is a string. The File class is a wrapper for the file name and its directory path.

slides.title: File Input and Output

blocks.text: A File object encapsulates the properties of a file or a path, but it does not contain the methods for reading/writing data from/to a file.
To perform file input and output (or I/O for short), you need to create objects using the appropriate Java I/O classes.
To read data from a text file, use the Scanner class.
To write data to a text file, use the PrintWriter class.
The Scanner and PrintWriter objects contain the methods for reading/writing data from/to a file.

slides.title: Reading Data using Scanner

blocks.text: The java.util.Scanner class was used to read strings and primitive values from the keyboard.
To read from the keyboard, create a Scanner object for

System.in, as follows:
Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
The Scanner class breaks its input into tokens separated by whitespace characters.
To read from a file, create a Scanner object for a file:
Scanner input = new Scanner(new File(filename));

slides.title: How does the Scanner Methods Work?

blocks.text: Token-based methods read input separated by delimiters:

next(), nextByte(), nextShort(), nextInt(),
nextLong(), nextFloat(), and nextDouble().
By default, the delimiters are whitespace characters.
A token-based input method skips any delimiters then reads a token ending at a delimiter.
However, nextLine() reads a complete line ending with a newline separator. The newline is read but is not part of the returned string.

slides.title: How does the Scanner Methods Work?

blocks.text: The token-based methods convert an input token into a primitive numeric value. For example:
nextByte() converts an input token into a byte.
nextInt() converts an input token into an int.
nextDouble() converts an input token into a double.
However, next() returns a string token without conversion.
If the token does not match the expected type, a runtime
java.util.InputMismatchException is thrown.

slides.title: Scanning a String

blocks.text: You can also use the Scanner class to scan a string.
Example:
String s = "12 13";
Scanner in = new Scanner(s);
int i = in.nextInt();
int j = in.nextInt();
int sum = i+j;
System.out.printf("i=%d, j=%d, sum=%d\n", i, j, sum);
